name: Shortcut Sheet
summary: Question mark opens a map of every shortcut on the page, read from the handlers themselves. A binding cannot exist without appearing here, and the sheet cannot list one that was removed.

attempts.prompt: Build a keyboard shortcuts modal that opens when you press question mark.
attempts.problem: The shortcut list was a hardcoded array inside the modal, entirely separate from the handlers that implement the shortcuts. That is the actual problem this component exists to solve: two lists that drift apart, so the sheet documents a binding that was removed six months ago and misses the three added last week. It also fired while the user was typing in a text field, so typing a question mark into a search box opened the modal.

attempts.prompt: Read the shortcuts from the DOM instead and ignore keys typed in inputs.
attempts.problem: Registration worked, but only single keys did. Sequence bindings of the g-then-d kind that every serious application uses were treated as literal two-character strings and never matched. There was also no distinction in the rendering between a sequence and a combination, so "g d" and "ctrl+d" were displayed identically despite being different things to press.

finalPrompt:
Build a keyboard shortcut sheet in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies.

The defining constraint: the sheet must be generated from the page, never from a list maintained alongside it. Every element carrying a data-shortcut attribute registers itself, and the sheet renders from that registry when it opens. A binding cannot exist without appearing in the sheet, and the sheet cannot document one that no longer exists. Group rows by a data-group attribute.

Support both kinds of binding and render them differently, because they are different things to press. A space-separated value like "g d" is a sequence: press g, then d. A plus-separated value like "shift+?" is a combination pressed together. Render each segment of a sequence as its own kbd element, and a combination as a single kbd with the parts joined.

Sequences need a buffer with a timeout of about 900ms. After each keystroke, test the buffer for an exact match and fire it; otherwise test whether any registered binding starts with the buffer plus a space, and clear the buffer if none does, so a stray key does not leave the matcher half-primed.

Never fire while the user is typing. Bail out at the top of the handler if the active element is an input, a textarea, or contenteditable. A question mark typed into a search field must reach the field.

The sheet is a real dialog: role="dialog", aria-modal, labelled by its heading, focus moved into it on open, Tab trapped inside, Escape to close, and focus restored to whatever was focused before.

Announce each fired shortcut through a role="status" element and emit a bubbling CustomEvent named ks:fire carrying the binding, so a host page can react without editing the component.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--bg), var(--surface), var(--raised), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent), var(--mono), with color-mix for the scrim. No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
The interesting failure here is not technical. The first attempt produced a perfectly working modal containing a hardcoded list — and a hardcoded list is exactly the thing that makes shortcut documentation useless after three months. The component looked complete and had no value.

What fixed it was stating the invariant rather than the feature: a binding cannot exist without appearing here, and the sheet cannot document one that was removed. That sentence forces registration from the DOM. Asking to read the shortcuts from the DOM would have got the same code, but the invariant also rules out the half-measures, like a registry that the sheet then overrides.

The second lesson is that a category distinction the model does not know it is making will be flattened. Sequences and combinations are different actions, and both get written as short strings, so a model treats them as one thing. Naming the two kinds, giving the syntax for each, and requiring them to render differently is the fix — and it is the same shape of correction as Enter versus Tab in the spreadsheet grid.
